course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 8

unit.title: Ecosystems
unit.blurb: Populations, communities and ecosystems, habitats and adaptations, seed banks, and how habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and bioaccumulation affect living things.

O1.t: Describe populations, communities and ecosystems, and identify the range of habitats in an ecosystem.

O2.t: Describe physical and behavioural adaptations, and explain why seed banks protect biodiversity.

O3.t: Explain how habitat destruction, overexploitation and invasive species affect organisms and ecosystems.

O4.t: Describe how pollution harms ecosystems and how toxic substances bioaccumulate along food chains.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 3: Ecosystems.
Bees carry pollen from flower to flower.
Without pollinators, many plants couldn't make seeds and fruit, and whole ecosystems,
including our food supply, would suffer.
Let's explore how living things depend on each other,
and how humans affect them.
A population is a group of organisms of one species living in an area,
like a herd of elephants.
A community is all the populations of different species living in the same area:
elephants, giraffes, zebras, trees and grasses together.
An ecosystem is the community plus all its interactions with non-living factors,
like light, water and temperature.
Organisms depend on each other for food and shelter.
An ecosystem can be as big as a mountain range,
or as small as a sealed glass jar!
There are many types of ecosystem.
Forests get lots of rain and have very varied life.
Grasslands are open, sunny and windy.
Deserts get little rain and lots of sun, with only a few producers.
Freshwater ecosystems include ponds, rivers and lakes and the land around them.
Saltwater ecosystems, the oceans, cover most of Earth's surface and include coral reefs.
Within an ecosystem there are many habitats.
A habitat is the place where a particular organism lives and thrives.
A deer's habitat is the forest,
but a tiny beetle's habitat might be the bark of a single tree.
Twelve woodlice are placed in the middle of a choice chamber.
One side is dry and light; the other side is damp and dark.
Predict: where will most of the woodlice be after ten minutes?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The woodlice crawl around the chamber for ten minutes.
Ten woodlice are now on the damp, dark side,
and only two are on the dry, light side.
Explain what you saw.
Woodlice lose water easily through their body covering,
so they survive best in damp places, like under logs and stones.
Moving away from light also helps them hide from predators.
This behaviour is an adaptation to their habitat.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
A class places square frames called quadrats at random in three parts
of the school field and counts the daisies in each one.
In full sun there are about 14 daisies per quadrat.
In part shade there are 8, and under the trees only 2.
Pause and decide: which non-living factor most likely affects where daisies grow,
and why do we use many quadrats placed at random?
Each organism has features that help it survive in its habitat.
These are adaptations. A forest monkey has physical adaptations: long, strong limbs for climbing,
a tail for balance and gripping branches, feet that grip like hands,
and teeth that grind leaves, seeds and fruit.
It also has a behavioural adaptation: living high in the treetops,
where there's food and protection from most predators.
A dolphin is adapted to the ocean.
It has a streamlined body,
a blowhole on top of its head for breathing,
fins and flippers to steer, a strong tail,
and a thick layer of blubber to keep warm.
Dolphins also have behavioural adaptations:
they live in groups called pods and communicate with each other.
Plants have adaptations too.
The resurrection plant curls up into a ball to survive drought,
then opens again when it rains!
Human activities and climate change threaten biodiversity.
Scientists estimate that two out of five plant species are endangered,
and losing them could threaten many other organisms and our food supply.
So botanists and geneticists store seeds in more than 1500 seed banks around the world.
Seeds are kept in the dark, with low humidity,
at about minus 20 degrees Celsius, so they won't start to grow.
Vaults like the Svalbard Global Seed Vault are protected from floods and earthquakes,
and every container is clearly labelled with the plant variety and where it was collected.

captions: Human activities are destroying natural habitats.
Forests are cut down for farms, logging and homes.
This is deforestation, and it's destroying the habitats of thousands of species.
Taking away one species affects a whole ecosystem.
Bats eat the fruit of banyan trees and spread their seeds.
Without banyan trees, bat numbers would fall,
and so would the owls and hawks that eat bats.
Forests are also carbon sinks, absorbing more carbon than they release,
so deforestation adds to climate change.
Roads, cities and farms can also break large habitats into small pieces.
This habitat fragmentation makes it harder for animals to find food,
water and shelter, and reduces biodiversity.
Overexploitation means removing too many animals from the wild,
for example by overfishing or overhunting.
When fish are caught faster than they can reproduce, populations fall,
and other organisms lose their food.
Some modern fishing methods scoop up everything from the ocean floor.
Sometimes humans bring a non-native species into an ecosystem.
The Nile perch was put into Lake Victoria in East Africa as food,
but it's a predator, and it wiped out many native fish species,
harming birds and mammals that ate them.
A non-native species that causes this much harm is called invasive.
Some species arrive by accident, with cargo and travellers.
Asian hornets prey on native bees, which are vital pollinators,
and rats on ships have driven many native birds to extinction.
On the positive side, re-introducing lost species, like wolves in Yellowstone National Park,
can help ecosystems recover.
Pollution harms ecosystems. Land pollution comes from litter,
plastics and chemicals that seep into the soil.
Rotting rubbish in landfills even releases methane, a greenhouse gas.
Air pollution comes from factory smoke, car exhausts and dust.
Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in clouds and make acid rain,
which harms plants and animals.
Water pollution comes from fertilisers, pesticides, factory chemicals, untreated waste water,
oil spills and litter.
Fertilisers make algae grow out of control, an algal bloom,
blocking sunlight so water plants die.
Oil sticks to feathers and fur, turtles swallow plastic bags,
and tiny microplastics have entered our food chains.
Two jars contain the same pond water.
A few drops of garden fertiliser are added to one jar.
Both are left in sunlight for two weeks.
Predict: what will happen?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Both jars stand in the same sunny place for two weeks.
The jar with fertiliser has turned bright green with algae.
The other jar is still almost clear.
Explain what you saw.
Fertiliser contains nutrients that help plants and algae grow.
When fertiliser washes off farmland into rivers and lakes,
algae grow very fast and cover the surface.
They block light, and when they die,
bacteria that decompose them use up the oxygen in the water,
so fish die. Pause and explain it in your own words.
This chart shows typical amounts of mercury in organisms along a polluted lake food chain,
in parts per million.
Plankton contain only a tiny amount.
Small fish have more, large fish more again,
and the fish-eating bird at the top has the most.
Pause and decide: why does the top predator
have so much more mercury than the plankton?
Some toxic substances, like mercury from mining and manufacturing,
can't be broken down or excreted.
When they get into water, tiny plankton absorb small amounts,
and it stays in their bodies.
This slow build-up is called bioaccumulation.
Small fish eat lots of plankton, so they take in more mercury.
Larger fish eat many small fish, so they get even more.
The amount gets higher and higher along the food chain.
This is biomagnification, and people who eat contaminated fish can get mercury poisoning.

Question 1: What is the difference between a population and a community?
Pause the video now.
Answer: A population is one species;
a community is all the populations in an area.
Question 2: Give one physical adaptation of a dolphin.
Pause the video now.
Answer: e.g. streamlined body, blowhole, blubber or flippers.
Question 3: What is an invasive species?
Pause the video now.
Answer: A non-native species that causes harm to its new ecosystem.
Question 4: Why do top predators have the most mercury in their bodies?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Biomagnification – mercury builds up along the food chain.

adv.prompt: * Advanced. A pollutant cannot be broken down. Each plankton contains 0.02 units of it. A small fish eats 500 plankton, and a tuna eats 40 small fish. How many units of the pollutant end up in the tuna?
adv.reason: One small fish: 500 × 0.02 = 10 units. Tuna: 40 × 10 = 400 units. The pollutant builds up along the food chain (bioaccumulation).
